title: Pressure-cooker pearl barley
subtitle: Tender, chewy barley in 20 minutes
excerpt: Pearl barley cooked under pressure until tender and slightly swollen, a versatile grain for soups, risotto-style dishes, grain bowls, and salads. The pressure cooker halves the usual stovetop cooking time.
sourceNotes: Pearl barley is polished barley with the outer husk removed. It has been used in British and Northern European cooking for centuries, in broths, stews, and porridges. It takes 35 to 45 minutes on the stovetop; the pressure cooker brings this to about 20 minutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool and freeze in airtight bags for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch and refrigerate for up to 4 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps refrigerated for up to 4 days. Use cold in salads or warm in soups and stews.

content.text: Pearl barley has a substantial, chewy texture that holds up well in soups, stews, and cold grain salads. On the stovetop it takes 35 to 45 minutes to cook through; the pressure cooker brings this to about 20 minutes and produces evenly cooked, plump grains without the risk of them sticking or catching on the base.

Pearl barley releases starch during cooking, so the cooking liquid turns slightly thick and cloudy. This is useful if cooking in stock for a soup or risotto-style dish, stir the barley into the liquid rather than draining it.

For a risotto-style dish (orzotto), cook the barley in stock with the sauté-then-pressure method: sauté aromatics first, add the barley, add stock, and pressure-cook. The result is creamy without constant stirring.

Put the rinsed pearl barley, {{stock-vegetable}} of vegetable stock, and salt in the pressure cooker. Stir once. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 10 minutes.

Open the lid and stir. The barley should be tender with a slight chew, it should not be mushy. If still firm, return to pressure for 5 more minutes. Use immediately in soup or a warm dish, or drain, cool rapidly, and refrigerate for use in cold grain salads.

rows.symptom: The barley is still firm after 20 minutes
rows.cause: Old stock, or the cooker did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for 5 more minutes with a splash of extra stock or water.

rows.symptom: The barley is very soft and mushy
rows.fix: Reduce to 15 minutes next time. For a less starchy result, drain and rinse after cooking.

content.text: Pearl barley is an underused British grain, historically the ingredient of Scotch broth, lamb stew, and winter soups before rice and pasta became the dominant staples. It holds its texture in soups, works as a risotto substitute (orzotto), and makes a better grain salad than couscous because it does not turn to mush. A batch cooked in stock provides a week's worth of grain that is more interesting than plain white rice.
